dialogues.patient_says: I'm fine. I'm just tired. I've been tired for about two years.

choices.text: Two years of tired is not just tired. What does your day usually look like?
Two years is a long time to push through. What keeps you going?
You should take a vacation.
Tired that lasts years is usually something more than tired. How did it start?

dialogues.patient_says: I used to care so much about my work. Now I feel nothing when I do it. Just going through the motions.

choices.text: That shift from caring to nothing is one of the clearest signs of burnout. When did you notice it happening?
What did caring about it feel like before?
Maybe you just need a new challenge.
Going through the motions takes its own kind of toll. Are you managing okay day to day?

dialogues.patient_says: I work twelve hour days and I still feel like I'm behind. It never ends.

choices.text: Twelve hours and still behind sounds like an impossible standard. Who set it?
What would happen if you worked ten hours instead?
You need to learn to manage your time better.
Behind according to who? You or someone else?

dialogues.patient_says: I can't remember the last time I did something just for fun. Not productive. Just fun.

choices.text: When fun starts feeling foreign that's the body telling you something is seriously out of balance.
What used to be fun before everything became about productivity?
Try to schedule some fun time into your week.
When did productivity become the only thing that counted?

dialogues.patient_says: People at work keep saying I seem checked out. I am. But I can't stop.

choices.text: Checked out but can't stop is a really painful place to be stuck. What feels like it would happen if you did stop?
What's keeping you in it?
You should talk to your manager about how you're feeling.
Showing up while completely empty takes more out of you than people realize.

dialogues.patient_says: I get irritated so easily now. Small things that never bothered me feel unbearable.

choices.text: When the tank is empty there's no buffer left. Irritability is often one of the first visible signs of burnout.
What's the kind of thing that sets you off lately?
Try to be more patient with yourself and others.
Small things feeling unbearable is the exhaustion talking. How long has the irritability been this bad?

dialogues.patient_says: I don't sleep well but I'm also exhausted all the time. Neither thing makes sense.

choices.text: It actually makes complete sense with burnout. The nervous system gets so overloaded it can't downshift even when the body is desperate for it.
What does your sleep look like? Do you wake up a lot or just not fall asleep?
Try cutting caffeine and sticking to a sleep schedule.
Your body and mind are both running on fumes. How long has this pattern been going on?

dialogues.patient_says: I feel guilty when I'm not working. Even on weekends. Even when I'm sick.

choices.text: That guilt has become its own kind of pressure on top of everything else. Where did it come from?
What do you think would happen if you rested without guilt?
You need to learn to switch off.
Resting while sick and feeling guilty about it is a sign the system is really out of balance.

dialogues.patient_says: I said yes to three more things this week even though I have no room. I don't know why I do that.

choices.text: Do you say yes to protect a relationship, avoid conflict, or because you genuinely think you can manage?
What would saying no feel like?
You need to start saying no.
Can you cancel any of them?

dialogues.patient_says: I used to be the most motivated person in my team. Now I can barely start anything.

choices.text: That contrast between who you were and who you feel like now must be really hard to sit with.
What does barely starting feel like? Is it resistance or just emptiness?
Maybe you just need some fresh inspiration.
The motivation didn't leave because something's wrong with you. It left because the tank has been dry for too long.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like a machine. Wake up, work, sleep, repeat. No feeling. Just function.

choices.text: When life becomes pure function the human part gets starved. What was the last thing that made you feel something?
How long has it felt like that?
Try adding something enjoyable to your routine.
Machines break down when they're run without maintenance. So do people.

dialogues.patient_says: I snapped at a colleague for something tiny. I apologized but I could see they were uncomfortable.

choices.text: You caught it and apologized. That matters. How did you feel after?
Is that happening more often lately?
You really need to manage your stress better at work.
That uncomfortableness from them on top of your own guilt sounds heavy.

dialogues.patient_says: I daydream about quitting constantly. I've never actually quit anything in my life.

choices.text: The daydream is telling you something even if acting on it isn't the right move yet. What does quitting feel like in the daydream?
What would you do if you did quit?
Don't quit. You'll regret it.
The fact that quitting feels like relief rather than failure says something about where you are.

dialogues.patient_says: I forgot to eat lunch three days in a row. I just didn't notice.

choices.text: Not noticing hunger is a sign your body is running in a kind of override mode. How are you feeling physically?
Are you eating enough outside of that?
Set an alarm for lunch.
When you stop hearing your own body's signals, that's the body hitting a limit.

dialogues.patient_says: My body aches all the time. My doctor said there's nothing wrong but it doesn't feel like nothing.

choices.text: Burnout has very real physical symptoms. Your body isn't lying to you.
Where does it ache?
If the doctor says you're fine then you're probably fine.
Chronic stress lives in the body. It doesn't always show up on tests.

dialogues.patient_says: I took a day off and spent it feeling guilty and checking my emails anyway.

choices.text: A day off that costs you the whole day in guilt isn't actually a day off. What made you check?
What would have happened if you hadn't checked?
You should put your phone in another room on your days off.
The inability to disconnect is a symptom not a character flaw.

dialogues.patient_says: I used to be able to think clearly. Now everything feels foggy.

choices.text: Cognitive fog is a very real burnout symptom. How long has it been hard to think clearly?
What kinds of things are hardest to think through right now?
Try meditating. It helps with focus.
The fog isn't permanent. But it is a signal that something needs to change.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I've lost my identity outside of work. I don't know who I am if I'm not producing something.

choices.text: When did work become the whole of who you are? Was there a version of you before that?
Who were you before work took over?
You need hobbies outside of work.
Your value doesn't come from what you produce. That's a hard thing to believe when productivity has been everything.

dialogues.patient_says: I left work on time yesterday. I actually left on time. It felt wrong.

choices.text: The fact that leaving on time felt wrong tells you how warped normal has become. How was the rest of the evening?
That's progress. What made today the day you left on time?
Good. Do it again tomorrow.
Leaving on time should feel normal. Let's work toward that.

dialogues.patient_says: I cried in the bathroom at work. Just for a minute. Then I went back to my desk.

choices.text: Crying in the bathroom and then going back is holding so much in such a small space. How often does that happen?
What brought it on?
It happens. Work can be stressful.
The minute you allowed yourself and then packed it back away. That's a hard thing to keep doing.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel resentful toward my job. I never used to feel that way.

choices.text: Resentment usually builds when you've given too much for too long without enough back. What does the resentment feel like?
What changed between then and now?
Maybe it's time to find a new job.
Resentment is information. What is it telling you?

dialogues.patient_says: I went for a walk this morning and felt almost human for a bit.

choices.text: Almost human is a start. What was the walk like?
That almost human feeling, what did it feel like exactly?
Good. You should walk every day.
Your body remembered something this morning. That's worth paying attention to.

dialogues.patient_says: I set a boundary with my boss today. I said I couldn't take on the extra project.

choices.text: That is genuinely difficult to do. How did they respond?
How did it feel to say no?
Be careful. You don't want to damage your reputation.
That took real courage. I'm proud of you.

dialogues.patient_says: I finished work at a reasonable time and read a book for an hour. I almost forgot I could do that.

choices.text: An hour of reading. Your brain had space to breathe. How did the rest of the evening feel?
What were you reading?
Good. Keep doing that.
You didn't forget. You were just too depleted to reach it. It's still there.

dialogues.patient_says: I've been thinking about whether any of this is worth it anymore. The job. Everything.

choices.text: When everything starts to feel not worth it that's worth paying close attention to. What does everything feel like right now?
Are you okay? When you say everything, what do you mean?
Of course it's worth it. You just need a break.
I want to understand what you mean by everything. Can you tell me more?

dialogues.patient_says: I had a conversation with a friend that had nothing to do with work. It felt so strange and also really good.

choices.text: Your brain got to exist outside of work mode for a bit. Strange and good is a really honest way to describe that.
What did you talk about?
You should make time for friends more often.
The good part of that is real. Hold onto it.

dialogues.patient_says: I slept in on Saturday. Actually slept in. I didn't set an alarm.

choices.text: Not setting an alarm and sleeping in is your body finally getting a small piece of what it needs. How did it feel?
What made you decide not to set one?
Sleeping in can mess up your sleep schedule.
I'm glad your body got that.

dialogues.patient_says: I'm starting to see that I've been doing this to myself as much as anything else has been doing it to me.

choices.text: That's a really significant insight. What does it feel like to see that?
What specifically do you think you've been doing?
Yes. You need to take responsibility for your limits.
Seeing your own part in it is not the same as blaming yourself. It means you have more agency than you thought.

dialogues.patient_says: I cooked a proper meal this week. Not just something fast. Something I actually wanted to eat.

choices.text: Cooking something you actually wanted is a sign your sense of desire is waking back up.
What did you make?
Good. Eating well is important for energy.
That's care for yourself. Real care. How did it feel?

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like I'm slowly coming back to life. It's very slow. But it's something.

choices.text: Slow is exactly right. Burnout doesn't recover fast and that's okay. What does coming back feel like?
What's different compared to a month ago?
Don't rush it.
Something is everything right now. I'm really glad.

dialogues.patient_says: I said no to overtime this week. First time in over a year.

choices.text: Over a year. That no cost you something to say. How did it feel?
What made this week the time to say it?
Good. Keep doing that.
That no was you choosing yourself. That's a big deal.

dialogues.patient_says: I noticed I was actually looking forward to something this week. A small thing. But I noticed.

choices.text: Looking forward to something is your brain starting to imagine a future again. What was the thing?
Small things are where it starts. What was it?
Good. Build on that.
The noticing matters as much as the thing itself.

dialogues.patient_says: I think I've been scared to slow down because I'm afraid of what I'll feel if I do.

choices.text: That fear is really common. Staying busy can be its own kind of armor. What do you think you'd feel?
What do you imagine is underneath the busyness?
You won't know until you try.
Whatever's there has been waiting. It won't be as bad with support as it would be alone.

dialogues.patient_says: I took a full weekend off. No work. Nothing. I didn't know what to do with myself at first.

choices.text: Not knowing what to do with yourself is what happens when work has been everything. What did you end up doing?
A full weekend. How did it feel by the end?
You should do that every weekend.
That disorientation at first is the system recalibrating. It's a good sign.

dialogues.patient_says: I feel like myself again in small moments. Not all the time. But sometimes.

choices.text: Sometimes is more than nothing. And small moments are where selves are rebuilt.
What does yourself feel like in those moments?
Keep working at it and it will come back fully.
I'm really glad to hear that.

dialogues.patient_says: I actually enjoyed a piece of work this week. A small piece. But I noticed it.

choices.text: The caring coming back even in a small piece is significant. What was it?
Enjoyed how? Like it felt meaningful or like it was just engaging?
See. It's not all bad.
Your relationship with work doesn't have to be all or nothing. That one piece shows you something.

dialogues.patient_says: I think I've started to understand what I actually need. Not just what I'm supposed to do.

choices.text: That distinction between what you need and what you're supposed to do is everything. What do you need?
What did you think you were supposed to do that you're questioning now?
Good. Act on it.
That kind of clarity is hard to get to. I'm glad you're there.

dialogues.patient_says: I think rest is starting to feel like rest again instead of just time I should be using.

choices.text: Rest feeling like rest is the whole thing. That shift took a long time.
What does rest feel like now compared to before?
Good. You needed that.
Your relationship with yourself is healing. That's what we've been working toward.

dialogues.patient_says: I don't think I'll go back to how I was before. I don't want to.

choices.text: Not wanting to go back is one of the most important things you could say. What will you do differently?
What was before that you don't want to return to?
Good. The old way wasn't sustainable.
That's the most important shift of all. You have a new normal now.

dialogues.patient_says: I actually feel okay today. Not managing. Not surviving. Just okay.

choices.text: Just okay after all of this is something worth sitting in for a moment.
Okay without the managing and surviving. That's new. How does it feel?
Good. Keep it up.
I'm really glad. You worked hard to get here.
